newsitem.title: INDIA: Mass cremation planned for India fire victims.
newsitem.headline: Mass cremation planned for India fire victims.

text.p: Indian authorities on Monday prepared a mass cremation for unidentified victims of a searing fire that killed at least 200 worshippers at a Hindu gathering.
Rescue workers began shifting corpses, charred beyond recognition, in trucks from the site of Sunday's inferno to a nearby cremation ground in the eastern town of Baripada, witnesses said.
"It will not be possible to identify all the bodies," deputy police chief P.K. Mishra said. "The administration will take unidentified bodies for mass cremation."

Authorities said they had identified only 49 of 168 bodies found in the debris of the inferno that engulfed makeshift bamboo and straw shelters at camp site in Baripada, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital of Orissa state, Bhubaneshwar.
Authorities said 32 of 187 injured had died in hospital.
It was not yet known when the bodies of the unidentified victims would, in line with Hindu custom, be cremated.
Panicked survivors searched for missing relatives.
"Relatives were crying desperately, looking for any information from police," said Sandeep Sahu.

"Women searched frantically because they did not know if their male relatives were alive," said P.K. Barik, a 46-year-old devotee who survived Sunday's blaze and was recovering in a hospital in nearby Cuttack town.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda flew to the spot, a football ground that was once the cremation site for the ruler of the region, the Maharaja of Mayurbhanj, who died on February 22, 1912 -- 85 years and one day before Sunday's fire.

Deve Gowda announced federal payments of 50,000 rupees ($1,400) to the victims' families and 25,000 rupees ($700) to the injured. The aid came on top of state payments of 25,000 rupees to the families of the deceased and 10,000 rupees to the injured.
Deve Gowda said the federal government would open discussions with religious leaders about ways to prevent a repeat of the tragedy.
The inferno erupted on the last day of a convention dedicated to a Hindu guru in Baripada, about 175 km (110 miles) southwest of Calcutta.

The flames, fanned by gusting winds, scorched the shelters for men devotees but spared a separate section for women and children. The cause of the fire was thought to be an electrical spark that quickly ignited the huts covered in dry straw.
"There was hardly any time to escape as the fire burnt down the camp within three minutes," said 27-year-old Dilip Kumar Mohapatra, who was recovering in a Cuttack hospital.
"There was a near stampede because everyone was trying to get out of the only gate."
The blaze highlighted the country's disregard for fire safety, officials said.

"It is kind of a casual approach, lack of accountability and no regard for safety," P.S. Das, additional director general of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), told Reuters in the capital New Delhi. BIS sets national technical standards.
India has no federal fire safety regulations. The BIS has recommended rules but the 26 states are free to adopt or reject them.

The state government launched an inquiry into what is believed to be the deadliest fire in India since December 1995 when about 425 people died when flames and smoke engulfed a school prize-giving ceremony in the northern town of Dabwali.
